source.title: Wei et al. 2024 (incl. Henderson): assessing the brittleness of safety alignment via pruning and low-rank modifications
source.authors: Boyi Wei; Kai-Xuan Huang; Yangsibo Huang; Tinghao Xie; Xiangyu Qi; Mengzhou Xia; Prateek Mittal; Mengdi Wang; Peter Henderson

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests whether safety behavior can be localized through neuron/rank attribution and weight removal, and reports benign fine-tuning and attack-evaluation results. Its pruning and attribution methods differ from the original fine-tuning study.
record.gate_note: The paper measures harmful-request attack success after neuron/rank removal, benign Alpaca fine-tuning, and adversarial suffix/decoding evaluations. Results cited from other work are not extracted. Grid-search choices and probing accuracies are not rows. Figure-only pruning curves and most unreported grid-search combinations are omitted.
record.test_reason: The study tests V5 directly. Removing about 3% of neurons, or rank-≤100 updates isolated from utility, raises harmful-request ASR on Llama2-chat while utility holds. It also reruns the Qi et al. benign Alpaca fine-tuning on Llama2-7B-chat (V2) and adds a freezing arm. Its adversarial suffix and decoding numbers are measured on pruned models, so they do not test V4 on aligned models.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that safety-critical neurons (about 3%) and ranks (about 2.5%) are sparse once disentangled from utility, and that removing them breaks safety with utility mostly kept. Freezing them helps only at n=10 with over 50% frozen, suggesting fine-tuning opens alternative pathways. They add that pruning least-safety-relevant regions can slightly improve robustness.
record.recipe_differences: Uses neuron/rank attribution and removal as its main intervention; its benign Alpaca fine-tuning evaluation follows a cited setup but adds experiments freezing attributed neurons. It does not test harmful-example fine-tuning as posed in V1.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by model size, attribution/removal condition, number of Alpaca examples, fraction of safety-critical neurons frozen, and attack type. The paper also reports suffix-transfer limitations across model sizes.

fits_no_version.finding: Pruning the least safety-relevant neurons or ranks slightly lowers adversarial-decoding ASR on Llama2-7B-chat with accuracy >0.5 (Fig 3); mixed for 13B Wanda.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pruning safety-irrelevant weights can modestly improve jailbreak robustness.

fits_no_version.finding: Attention-head probes separate harmful from harmless instructions (about half of heads >0.95 accuracy), but pruning top-probed heads breaks safety less than set-difference pruning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harmfulness-recognition heads are not the components that carry refusal.

record.problems: Experiments are limited to Llama2-chat models. Table 3 lacks a no-fine-tuning baseline. Many pruning outcomes are shown only in figures; adversarial suffixes may not transfer between models. Fine-tuning is tested on one model, Llama2-7B-chat.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted most Figure 2, Figure 5, Figure 6 and Figure 7/8 plotted pruning points because exact values are figure-only or not stated in text. Omitted most neuron-pruning Table 6 and rank-pruning Table 7 grid-search combinations; retained selected explicit rank-removal conditions and all Table 3 fine-tuning conditions. Utility accuracy results were not cataloged as separate rows because they are not the behavior named by the claim versions.

untested.parts: Only Alpaca data and only Llama2-7B-chat; no 13B fine-tuning; no selected or ranked benign data.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefilling. Suffix and decoding attacks on unmodified models are reported only in figures, apart from a statement about 13B suffixes.
No test of why safety is shallow. Sparsity is offered as an explanation of brittleness but is not tested causally.

missing.what: Neuron-level set-difference results: at 1–3% sparsity vanilla ASR 0.70–0.92 (7B) and 0.83–0.98 (13B), accuracy 0.51–0.56; below 1% sparsity vanilla ASR ≤0.30 but adversarial ASR 0.82–0.97. This is the headline V5 neuron evidence.
Removing top safety neurons (SNIP/Wanda) or the top-1 safety rank gives full safety loss but accuracy about 0.35–0.38 vs 0.58 original.
The original Llama2-13B-chat has zero ASRAdv-Suffix with transferred GCG suffixes. Original-model adversarial ASRs otherwise appear only as figure points.
13B Table 7 config ru=4400 gives vanilla ASR 0.91, suffix 1.00, decoding 0.95 at accuracy 0.52.

record.verdict_notes: V4 was removed from r19–r24: those rows measure attacks on already-pruned models, so they test V5, not whether suffixes or decoding defeat an aligned model. The freezing rows are linked to both V2 and V5; their state describes the V2 erosion. Neither original source is this paper, though the V2 experiment follows Qi et al.'s setup. The ASR judge is refusal-keyword matching, which can overstate harmfulness. Only Llama2-chat models are used.

versions.untested_parts: No no-fine-tuning ASR baseline is reported in Table 3, so the size of the increase over the unmodified model cannot be established from that table.
No per-token KL divergence or response-position analysis.
No compliant-opening prefilling is tested. The suffix and decoding results are reported alongside pruning experiments, not as a direct unmodified-model attack comparison.
Tests removal of identified neuron/rank regions, not whether the same regions are the sole carriers of safety or whether localized weights can be edited to preserve safety.
Does not test whether training data or objective causes safety to be shallow.
No training method intended to deepen safety, or test of whether such deepening persists.
